title: Renewing Marriage, Revitalizing the Faith: Insights from the Vatican Meeting https://ifstudies.org/blog/renewing-marriage-revitalizing-the-faith-insights-from-the-vatican-meeting
author: J.P. De Gance
summary: J.P. De Gance, founder of Communio, reports on the Vatican's October meeting on marriage and the family, convened by Pope Leo XIV on the tenth anniversary of Amoris Laetitia, and argues that the marriage crisis is at root a worldview crisis. He points to survey data in which most American parents want their children to be financially independent and fulfilled in a career but few say marriage matters, and links this to consumerism and what Brad Wilcox calls the Midas Mindset. Citing IFS research that devout married couples report the happiest marriages, he contends that adapting Christian teaching to the moment has not produced growth in mainline denominations. He also reports that most priests and Mass attendees grew up in intact married families and concludes that faith revival requires marriage renewal in the pews. The argument is advocacy from a faith-based organization, supported by selected survey figures.
points: Bishops from several continents described the same worldview crisis around marriage that appears in the United States.
Survey data show 9 in 10 American parents want their kids to be financially independent with a fulfilling career, while only 1 in 5 say it matters that they marry.
The author ties the marriage crisis to consumerism and the primacy of career success in the search for meaning.
Communio data report that 83% of US Sunday Mass attendees grew up in an intact married family, and the marriage rate has fallen 65 percent since 1970.
He concludes that any pastor can start renewal by teaching the Christian view of marriage and family from the pulpit, and by helping young people learn to discern and live marriage well.
quotes: Fundamentally, the marriage crisis is a worldview crisis. Whether one wants to talk about feminism or consumerism, the dominant view in our culture places career success at center stage of life’s search for meaning.

We see this worldview clearly in research data where 9 in 10 American parents now say it is important their kids grow up to be financially independent and have a fulfilling career —but just 1 in 5 say it’s important that they get married.
This view forgets that the most meaningful and fulfilled lives are ones enriched by the deepest relationships, not career achievements.
This research builds on an avalanche of secular data showing the growth in nearly every social pathology is associated with the decline of marriage in the population.
Going beyond the pulpit to the pews, Communio survey data reveals that 83% of Sunday Mass attendees in the U.S. grew up in an intact married family.

The decline in Catholic priestly vocations and in the number of Sunday Mass attendees occurred after the share of adults raised outside of marriage began to grow. Just since 1970, the annual marriage rate has shrunk by 65 percent.

This means that the marriage crisis is the efficient cause of the crisis in faith practice. For church leaders—Protestant as well as Catholic—there is no path to sustained faith revival without the renewal of marriage in the pews.
Any pastor or church can begin this work immediately, by teaching the Christian worldview on marriage and family from the pulpit.
